subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Palmyra: Pearl of the Desert
description: A short lesson to help you apply Palmyra: Pearl of the Desert.

hook.text: Palmyra was a Roman trading city in the Syrian desert ruled briefly by a queen who defied an emperor.

buildup.text: Queen Zenobia declared independence from Rome in 270 CE and conquered Egypt before Rome crushed her revolt.

discovery.text: Its colonnaded streets, temples, and tombs survived 1,700 years of abandonment in remarkable condition.

twist.text: In 2015, ISIS destroyed the Temple of Bel and other monuments, erasing what centuries of neglect could not.

climax.text: 3D scans made before the destruction are now being used to digitally reconstruct what was lost.

punchline.text: A queen defied Rome and lost. A city defied time and almost won.

quiz.question: What happened to Palmyra's ancient monuments in 2015?
options: An earthquake damaged several major structures
ISIS destroyed the Temple of Bel and other monuments
Flooding from a nearby dam submerged part of the ruins

details.summary: Palmyra, a wealthy oasis city in the Syrian desert, thrived as a trade hub between Rome and Persia from the 1st to 3rd centuries CE. Its monumental colonnaded streets, temples, and tower tombs blended Greco-Roman and eastern art. ISIS destroyed parts of it in 2015.
details.whyItMatters: Palmyra's deliberate destruction by ISIS demonstrated that cultural heritage remains a target in modern warfare. The international outcry highlighted the connection between cultural destruction and the erasure of communities.
takeaways: A wealthy trade city blending Roman and eastern architectural styles
Thrived as a crossroads between Rome and Persia for centuries
ISIS deliberately destroyed key monuments in 2015

faq.question: What did ISIS destroy at Palmyra?
faq.answer: ISIS demolished the Temple of Bel (1st century CE), the Temple of Baalshamin, the Arch of Triumph, and several tower tombs. They also executed Palmyra's 82-year-old chief archaeologist Khaled al-Asaad, who had protected the site for over 50 years and refused to reveal where objects were hidden.

faq.question: Can Palmyra be rebuilt?
faq.answer: Partial reconstruction is underway using photogrammetric data, historical photographs, and 3D models created before the destruction. Some archaeologists argue that ruins should be left as evidence of destruction rather than reconstructed.
